source_text: Nam cum proponerent Ariani, qui rerum ea tempestate potiebantur, Homousion sequi vultis, aut Christum? Responderunt continuo, quasi in nomen religiosi, Christum se sequi; homousion repudiavere; atque ita exeunt gestientes, velut qui Christo crederent, quem iam negaverant, homousion, id est unius cum Patre substantiae, denegando. Ita ergo et nunc vos fabricatores doli, imperitas terretis aures, ut si nolunt laborantium pro fide virorum appellatione respergi, et liberum arbitrium negent, et Deum hominum conditorem. Hoc igitur a me in illo loco constat obiectum; et quam non falso, praesens disputatio palam faciet. Respondisti ergo hoc modo: Non negamus liberum arbitrium; et nihil aliud subiunxisti de tuo. Consequens enim fuerat, ut impleres sine tergiversatione sententiam; cumque praemisisses non te negare arbitrii libertatem, adderes: Sed confitemur datam a Deo libertatem arbitrii in hominum permanere natura.
pass_a_gloss: For when the Arians, who at that season were potently holding things, were proposing, Do you want to follow Homousion, or Christ? They answered at once, as if unto a religious name, that they follow Christ; they repudiated homousion; and so they go out rejoicing, as if who believed Christ, whom they had already denied, by denying homousion, that is of one substance with the Father. So therefore also now you fabricators of trick, terrify unskilled ears, that if they are unwilling to be sprinkled with the naming of men laboring for the faith, they deny both free choice and God the founder of humans. This therefore stands as objected by me in that place; and how not falsely, the present disputation will make open. You answered therefore in this manner: We do not deny free choice; and you joined nothing else of your own. For it had been consequent, that you fill the sentence without tergiversation; and when you had sent ahead that you do not deny the liberty of choice, you would add: But we confess that the liberty of choice given by God remains in the nature of humans.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS conditor; Blaise God as maker from nothing
Blaise homoousion; Greek loan in Latin controversy

pass_b_english: The Arians, who held power at that time, put the question: “Do you wish to follow ‘of one substance’, or Christ?” They immediately answered, as though devoutly loyal to the name, that they followed Christ; they rejected “of one substance”. And so they left rejoicing as though they believed in Christ, whom they had already denied by rejecting “of one substance”, that is, of one substance with the Father. In the same way you now manufacture deceit and frighten uneducated ears, so that if people do not want to be stained with the names of men who struggle for the faith, they must deny both free choice and God as humanity's Creator. This is plainly the charge I made in that passage. The present discussion will openly show how true it was. You therefore answered: “We do not deny free choice”, and added nothing further of your own. Consistency required you to complete your statement without evasion. Having begun by saying that you did not deny freedom of choice, you should have added: “Rather, we confess that the freedom of choice given by God remains in human nature.”

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
